hypotheses.title: CP-005 TOCTOU: Double-Update Race via initialized=false Re-fetch Trigger
hypotheses.mechanism: setTokenSettings (CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.sol:357-401) creates memSettings with initialized=true for registry storage (line 376-378), but broadcasts the ORIGINAL `settings` calldata (initialized=false when caller omits the flag) to hooks at line 397 via registryUpdateTokenSettings. AMMStandardHook.registryUpdateTokenSettings (line 519-525) writes this verbatim — hook cache gets initialized=false. On the next swap, _getOrFetchTokenSettings (lines 907-919) detects initialized=false and re-fetches the CURRENT registry state. If a SECOND setTokenSettings call has been submitted between the first broadcast and this lazy re-fetch (e.g., two admin txs in the same block, or a griefing attack that sandwiches the first update), the hook applies the second update's parameters — fee rates, whitelist IDs, trading pause — even though both parties intended sequential application. The desync window is any mempool time between first registryUpdateTokenSettings and the next hook interaction.
hypotheses.grounded_in: CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.sol:397 sends `settings` (initialized=false) instead of `memSettings` (initialized=true) to hooks; AMMStandardHook.sol:910 re-fetches when initialized=false; registry getTokenSettings (line 894-896) always returns initialized=true after set.

coupled_pair.invariant: Hook's initialized flag must mirror registry's initialized flag; false flag triggers re-fetch that can apply an out-of-order settings update

masking_code.masks_invariant: 'if (_tokenSettings[token].initialized)' appears as a gas optimization but is actually a TOCTOU gate masked by CP-005 — readers assume the broadcast always sets initialized=true, hiding the race window

hypotheses.impact: Admin or protocol can accidentally or maliciously apply out-of-order settings updates to a hook. Token-specific fee rates, whitelist IDs, or trading pause flags could revert to a stale or second-update value mid-block if two setTokenSettings transactions land back-to-back.

hypotheses.title: New Hook Deployment Bypasses All Pricing Bounds: Lazy Fetch Omits _pricingBounds
hypotheses.mechanism: _getOrFetchTokenSettings (AMMStandardHook.sol:907-919) populates the hook's _tokenSettings cache when initialized=false by calling SETTINGS_REGISTRY.getTokenSettings(token) (line 912). This function returns only the HookTokenSettings struct — it NEVER fetches or populates _pricingBounds[token][pairedToken] in the hook. When a new AMMStandardHook is deployed and associated with an existing token that already has pricing bounds set in the registry (via setPricingBounds, lines 482-526), the hook's _pricingBounds mapping is empty (isSet=false for all pairs). _validatePricingBounds (lines 823-871) begins with 'if (!_pricingBounds[token][pairedToken].isSet) { return; }' at line ~830 — when isSet=false, the ENTIRE bounds check is silently skipped. An attacker who observes the gap (registry has bounds, hook has isSet=false) can execute swaps or add liquidity at prices that should be blocked by the registry-configured min/maxSqrtPriceX96 bounds, causing maximal impermanent loss to LPs who expected price-range protection.
hypotheses.grounded_in: AMMStandardHook._getOrFetchTokenSettings (lines 907-919) calls getTokenSettings() only — not getPricingBounds(); _validatePricingBounds (line ~830) returns silently when isSet=false; CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.setPricingBounds (lines 482-526) does not auto-push to hooks unless hooksToSync includes them.

coupled_pair.invariant: If registry has isSet=true for a token pair, every active hook must also have isSet=true before processing any operations for that pair

masking_code.masks_invariant: 'if (!_pricingBounds[token][pairedToken].isSet) { return; }' looks like a benign early-exit for uninitialized pairs but is the bypass gate activated whenever pricing bounds were never synced to the hook

hypotheses.impact: New hook deployment during active token operation leaves a price bounds bypass window. An attacker can monitor deployment transactions and front-run the syncPricingBounds call to execute swaps or add liquidity at extreme prices. Even without an attacker, the window exists until admin manually calls syncPricingBounds.

hypotheses.title: Whitelist ID Rotation DoS: Hook Content Empty After ID Change
hypotheses.mechanism: When an admin calls setTokenSettings with a new lpWhitelistId (e.g., changing from ID=5 to ID=6), the new HookTokenSettings struct is broadcast to hooks via registryUpdateTokenSettings (lines 519-525). The hook stores lpWhitelistId=6. However, the hook's local _lpWhitelists[6] mapping is empty — only whitelist 5's content was previously synced. AMMStandardHook.validateAddLiquidity (lines 243-279) checks _lpWhitelists[tokenSettings.lpWhitelistId].contains(caller). Since _lpWhitelists[6] is empty, every LP address fails and is rejected with AMMStandardHook__LiquidityProviderNotAllowed. The content for whitelist 6 must be explicitly pushed via a separate updateLpWhitelist call with hooksToSync — there is no auto-content sync when the whitelist ID changes in tokenSettings. The same pattern applies to pairedTokenWhitelistId and poolTypeWhitelistId changes.
hypotheses.grounded_in: AMMStandardHook.validateAddLiquidity (lines 243-279) reads _lpWhitelists[tokenSettings.lpWhitelistId]; registryUpdateTokenSettings (lines 519-525) stores new lpWhitelistId but NOT whitelist content; CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.updateLpWhitelist (lines 689-710) is a separate mandatory call.

coupled_pair.state_b: AMMStandardHook._lpWhitelists[newId] (empty — content never pushed) AND AMMStandardHook._tokenSettings[token].lpWhitelistId (updated to newId)
coupled_pair.invariant: When lpWhitelistId changes, the hook's local content for the new ID must be populated before any liquidity operations proceed

masking_code.masks_invariant: lpWhitelistId stored inside HookTokenSettings struct looks like 'just another settings field', hiding the fact that it points to a separate local mapping requiring independent content sync

hypotheses.impact: Admin rotating whitelist IDs (common operational action) creates a DoS on addLiquidity for ALL LPs until explicit content sync. In a high-throughput environment, this could block LP operations for multiple blocks. Grieving attack: front-run syncLpWhitelist to keep DoS window open.

hypotheses.title: Whitelist Content Bypass: Revoked Member Passes Stale Hook Cache
hypotheses.mechanism: CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.updateLpWhitelist (lines 689-710) updates the registry's master _lpWhitelists content and OPTIONALLY notifies hooks (hooksToSync parameter). When called with hooksToSync=[] (empty), the registry removes the address from its authoritative list but does NOT call registryUpdateWhitelistLpAddress on any hook. AMMStandardHook._enforceLiquidityModificationSettings (or equivalent validateAddLiquidity check, lines 243-279) reads only the hook's LOCAL _lpWhitelists[lpWhitelistId].contains(provider). Since the hook's cache was not updated, the revoked address continues to pass the check. The same vulnerability applies to updatePairTokenWhitelist and updatePoolTypeWhitelist. A sophisticated actor who detects they are being removed from the registry whitelist (by monitoring emitted events) can continue using the hook until it is explicitly synced.
hypotheses.grounded_in: AMMStandardHook.validateAddLiquidity reads _lpWhitelists at lines 243-279; CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.updateLpWhitelist hooksToSync[] is caller-controlled and can be empty (lines 689-710); hook has no pull mechanism to detect registry-side changes.

coupled_pair.invariant: Removal of an address from the registry's authoritative whitelist must propagate to every active hook's local cache before further operations by that address

hypotheses.impact: Admin banning a malicious LP from the registry whitelist does not immediately revoke access. The banned address can continue adding liquidity (manipulating pool state or extracting fees) until admin explicitly syncs each hook. In security-sensitive contexts (sanctions compliance, incident response), this delay is critical.

hypotheses.title: validateHandlerOrder Reads Stale Local Pricing Bounds — No Registry Fallback
hypotheses.mechanism: AMMStandardHook.validateHandlerOrder (lines 198-226) is an `external view` function called by transfer handlers (CLOB, permit) during order creation. It reads _pricingBounds[token][pairedToken] from the hook's LOCAL cache (around line 210). Unlike beforeSwap, afterSwap, validateAddLiquidity, and validatePoolCreation — which all call _getOrFetchTokenSettings that can refresh the HookTokenSettings cache — validateHandlerOrder does NOT call _getOrFetchTokenSettings and does NOT make any live call to SETTINGS_REGISTRY. If pricing bounds were tightened in the registry (via setPricingBounds with empty hooksToSync), the hook's _pricingBounds cache remains stale. Handler orders at prices outside the new tight bounds continue to pass validation. External integrators calling validateHandlerOrder receive incorrect validation results.
hypotheses.grounded_in: AMMStandardHook.validateHandlerOrder (lines 198-226) reads _pricingBounds[token][pairedToken] directly — no _getOrFetchTokenSettings call, no SETTINGS_REGISTRY call; CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.setPricingBounds (lines 482-526) hooksToSync is optional.

coupled_pair.invariant: validateHandlerOrder must enforce the current registry pricing bounds, not stale hook-local cache

masking_code.masks_invariant: 'external view' signature makes validateHandlerOrder appear as a live safety check; staleness of local bounds cache is not apparent and not documented

hypotheses.impact: Admin tightens pricing bounds in response to price manipulation but forgets to sync the hook. CLOB handlers or limit-order systems using this validation approve orders at the old (wider) bounds. When those orders fill, counterparties execute at prices the admin intended to block.

hypotheses.title: checkDisabledPools Flag Desync: Disabled Pool Not Enforced When Hook Cache Is Stale
hypotheses.mechanism: _checkPoolEnabled (AMMStandardHook.sol:651-657) makes a live cross-contract call to SETTINGS_REGISTRY.isPoolDisabled(poolId) ONLY when tokenSettings.checkDisabledPools is true. The checkDisabledPools flag comes from the LOCAL hook cache (_tokenSettings[token]) — it is NOT re-fetched from the registry in real time. CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.setPoolDisabled (lines 417-452) updates _disabledPools[poolId] in the registry but has NO mechanism to push to hooks or invalidate caches. If the hook's cached checkDisabledPools=false (due to old settings or a missed sync), the entire disabled-pool check is skipped via the guard at AMMStandardHook.sol:652. Admin calling setPoolDisabled to emergency-halt a pool is completely ineffective for swaps on hooks where checkDisabledPools is cached as false.
hypotheses.grounded_in: _checkPoolEnabled (lines 651-657) conditionally calls SETTINGS_REGISTRY.isPoolDisabled based on cached tokenSettings.checkDisabledPools; CreatorHookSettingsRegistry.setPoolDisabled (lines 417-452) only updates registry; no push mechanism to hooks.

coupled_pair.invariant: If a pool is disabled in the registry, the hook must enforce that disable regardless of cached checkDisabledPools flag value

masking_code.masks_invariant: 'if (tokenSettings.checkDisabledPools)' looks like a feature toggle / gas optimization; when cached as false the live registry disabled-pool check is silently skipped, allowing trading in a pool the registry considers emergency-halted

hypotheses.impact: Admin disables a pool (e.g., exploit response, oracle failure) and enables checkDisabledPools, but hook's cached flag is false from old settings. All swaps continue through the disabled pool. Financial impact depends on the emergency scenario — ranging from continued exploit drainage to failed circuit-breaker protection.

hypotheses.title: Direct Swap Shared Transient Slot Cross-Token Collision (L-04 Multi-Token Extension)
hypotheses.mechanism: DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (AMMStandardHook.sol:66) is a single shared transient storage slot used by _validatePricingBounds for ALL direct swaps (poolType==address(0)). In beforeSwap, line ~839 stores params.amount via _setTstorish(DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT, params.amount). In afterSwap, line ~843-844 reads the slot to compute execution price. The slot is NEVER reset between calls (Guardian L-04, acknowledged). The novel extension: if a single AMMStandardHook instance serves two tokens (tokenA and tokenB) both with pricing bounds, and a single transaction triggers beforeSwap(tokenA) → beforeSwap(tokenB) → afterSwap(tokenA), then tokenB's beforeSwap overwrites the slot set by tokenA's beforeSwap. tokenA's afterSwap reads tokenB's amount and validates price against a fabricated (tokenA_amount_in / tokenB_amount_in) ratio instead of the actual tokenA execution price. With precisely chosen amounts, this allows tokenA to pass pricing bounds it would normally fail.
hypotheses.grounded_in: AMMStandardHook.sol:66 DIRECT_SWAP_BEFORE_SWAP_AMOUNT_SLOT single shared slot; _validatePricingBounds:~839 _setTstorish in beforeSwap; _validatePricingBounds:~843-844 _getTstorish in afterSwap; no clear/reset; Guardian L-04 acknowledged but limited to single-token scope.

coupled_pair.invariant: Each token's direct swap before-amount must be isolated from other tokens' direct swaps within the same transaction

masking_code.masks_invariant: 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF looks like a collision-resistant 'magic' slot address, obscuring that it is a single global slot shared across ALL token pairs simultaneously

hypotheses.impact: Low confidence due to multi-token same-tx direct swap requirement being unusual. If achievable, attacker crafts amounts such that tokenB's amount makes tokenA's price ratio appear within bounds when it actually exceeds them. Severity: medium (bypasses a safety check) if attack path is constructible.
